chief_complaint: change in bowel habits, rectal bleeding, and feeling wiped out for 3 months
hpi_details: 3-month history of progressive change in bowel habits from normal daily stools to looser, frequent stools mixed with dark blood and mucus. Reports sensation of incomplete evacuation (tenesmus) and crampy lower abdominal discomfort. Has lost 5kg unintentionally without dieting and feels exhausted climbing stairs.
ideas: thinks his old internal haemorrhoids have flared up again
concerns: deeply worried about bowel cancer as his brother was diagnosed at age 65
expectations: wants a quick check-up and ointment for bleeding, but also wants to know the truth immediately
pmh: internal haemorrhoids diagnosed 10 years ago, type 2 diabetes, hyperglycaemia
social_hx: smoker 25 pack-years, drinks 15 units alcohol/week, retired civil servant

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Colorectal Adenocarcinoma (suspected) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Urgent suspected cancer pathway referral for full colonoscopy and biopsies, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: change in bowel habits, rectal bleeding, and feeling wiped out for 3 months

Key HPI features: 3-month history of progressive change in bowel habits from normal daily stools to looser, frequent stools mixed with dark blood and mucus. Reports sensation of incomplete evacuation (tenesmus) and crampy lower abdominal discomfort. Has lost 5kg unintentionally without dieting and feels exhausted climbing stairs.

Objective/Exam findings: Abdominal exam, digital rectal examination (DRE) to palpate for low rectal mass. Bloods: FBC (microcytic iron deficiency anaemia typical), ferritin, renal profile, LFTs, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA baseline). Urgent two-week-wait colonoscopy and staging CT thorax/abdomen/pelvis.
Relevant background/PMH: internal haemorrhoids diagnosed 10 years ago, type 2 diabetes, hyperglycaemia
Current medications: metformin 1000mg BD, aspirin 75mg OD
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Colorectal Adenocarcinoma (suspected).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Complicated diverticular disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Unintentional weight loss with rectal bleeding — together they raise suspicion of malignancy over haemorrhoids.
management_principles: Urgent suspected cancer pathway referral for full colonoscopy and biopsies
Hold aspirin if biopsy/polypectomy anticipated after discussing vascular risk
Communicate clinical suspicion gently and transparently, ensuring support system involvement
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 68M with 3-month history of progressive change in bowel habits from normal daily stools to looser, frequent stools mixed with dark blood and mucus. Reports sensation of incomplete evacuation (tenesmus) and crampy lower abdominal discomfort. Has lost 5kg unintentionally without dieting and feels exhausted climbing stairs.
reference_soap.objective: Abdominal exam, digital rectal examination (DRE) to palpate for low rectal mass. Bloods: FBC (microcytic iron deficiency anaemia typical), ferritin, renal profile, LFTs, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA baseline). Urgent two-week-wait colonoscopy and staging CT thorax/abdomen/pelvis.
reference_soap.assessment: Suspected colorectal adenocarcinoma (rectosigmoid lesion likely). DDx: complicated diverticular disease, large adenomatous polyp, inflammatory bowel disease, severe haemorrhoidal bleeding (unlikely alone given systemic signs).
reference_soap.plan: Urgent suspected cancer pathway referral for full colonoscopy and biopsies. Hold aspirin if biopsy/polypectomy anticipated after discussing vascular risk. Communicate clinical suspicion gently and transparently, ensuring support system involvement.

learning_objectives: Elicit comprehensive colorectal cancer red flags: tenesmus, mixed PR blood, persistent bowel habit change, weight loss
Perform thorough family history risk stratification for hereditary non-polyposis/adenomatous polyposis
Explain the rationale behind urgent two-week-wait endoscopy pathways to an anxious patient
Manage patient fixation on benign explanations (haemorrhoids) while maintaining diagnostic vigilance

teaching.one_liner: A tumour in the rectum or sigmoid colon bleeds intermittently and narrows the bowel, causing a change in bowel habit, blood mixed in the stool, and weight loss.
red_flags: Unintentional weight loss with rectal bleeding — together they raise suspicion of malignancy over haemorrhoids

must_ask.say: How has your bowel habit changed — are your stools looser or more frequent than before?
Is the blood mixed into the stool, or just on the surface or on the toilet paper?
Do you feel like you still need to go, even right after a bowel movement?
Have you lost weight without trying to, or without dieting?
Have you noticed feeling more exhausted, like getting short of breath climbing stairs?
You mentioned your brother had bowel cancer — at what age was he diagnosed?
What are you most worried this might be?
